name: Lapita culture
title: The story of the Lapita culture

text: About 3,300 years ago, the Lapita people appeared on islands north-east of New Guinea.
Their ancestors were farmers and seafarers who had come from the islands of Southeast Asia.
src: The Lapita culture ... appeared in the Bismarck Archipelago north-east of New Guinea between about 1500 and 1300 BCE
Descended largely from Austronesian voyagers of Island Southeast Asia / the expansion of Austronesian-speaking farmers and seafarers

text: They are known for pottery stamped with tiny dots, made with toothed tools like small combs.
Some pots show faces, which many scholars think are pictures of ancestors.
src: potters pressed toothed tools, like small combs, into the damp surface to make lines of tiny dots, a technique called dentate stamping
Among them are stylised human faces / Many scholars also read the stylised human faces on the finest pots as images of ancestors

text: In sailing canoes with outriggers, they crossed hundreds of kilometres of open sea.
They became the first people to live on Vanuatu, New Caledonia, Fiji, Tonga and Samoa.
src: they built outrigger canoes, and perhaps double-hulled ones, able to cross hundreds of kilometres of open sea
its seafarers crossed hundreds of kilometres of open ocean to become the first people of Vanuatu, New Caledonia, Fiji, Tonga and Samoa

text: They built small villages by the sea, where they fished and grew taro, yams and bananas.
They brought pigs, dogs and chickens with them to the new islands.
src: Lapita communities lived by the sea / Most settlements seem to have been hamlets or small villages / They lived by fishing, gathering shellfish and farming / They grew taro, yams, bananas and breadfruit
The Lapita people brought pigs, dogs and chickens

text: They made fishhooks, rings and beads from shells.
They carried obsidian, a sharp volcanic glass, thousands of kilometres across the sea.
src: fishhooks of shell, and ornaments: rings, armbands, beads and discs, many of them cut from cone shells
Obsidian, a volcanic glass prized for its sharp edges / Talasea obsidian reached Vanuatu, New Caledonia and Fiji, thousands of kilometres to the south-east

text: Their descendants in Tonga and Samoa became the Polynesians.
Much later, Polynesian voyagers settled faraway islands such as Hawaii, New Zealand and Rapa Nui.
src: their descendants in Tonga and Samoa became the Polynesians
From these islands, after a long interval, voyagers set out to settle East Polynesia from about the 11th century CE, reaching the Society Islands, the Marquesas, Hawaii, Rapa Nui and New Zealand
